988.title: The priest and the big bang
988.word: The priest and the big bang
988.hook: Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, proposed the expanding universe
988.howItsDone: Christians hold a range of views on how scripture and science fit together; the Catholic Church has its own academy of sciences, and Christians work as scientists across many fields.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a pope's letter that opened with a song, and a garden handed over to be kept. Your line was our common home. What one small thing did you keep? Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

A man in a black clerical collar stands at a blackboard covered in equations. He is a Catholic priest. He is also a physicist, trained in the mathematics of Einstein's theory of gravity. And the equations are telling him something strange. The universe isn't standing still. It's getting bigger. Run the film backward, he reasons, and everything gets closer and closer together, until it all begins from one small, dense starting point. He called it a primeval atom. Other people later gave it a nickname, and the nickname stuck. His name was Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest. Today, the priest and the big bang.

The first line of the Bible, in the King James translation, is "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." A few lines later: "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light." It would be easy to hear Lemaître's idea, a universe with a beginning, and say: there it is, Genesis proved by physics. Lemaître himself didn't want anyone to say that. When church voices began to treat his theory as scientific proof of creation, he pushed back, quietly but firmly. His reasoning, as it's usually reported, ran like this. Physics describes how the universe unfolds. It can't tell you whether there is a God. And the Bible, he said, wasn't written to teach science; it was written to teach the way to salvation. Keep the two in their own lanes, and neither one has to be afraid of the other. He spent his life in both. He said Mass and he did mathematics, and he didn't think he was being torn in half. Christians have held a range of views on faith and science, and they still do. Some read Genesis as a literal account of how the world was made. Others read it as a different kind of truth, about who made the world and why. Lemaître's own path was to study the heavens as closely as he could, and to keep praying. There's an old psalm that sits well beside his blackboard: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." The psalm doesn't do the math. It looks up, and it praises.
screen: `THE HEAVENS DECLARE THE GLORY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up at the sky. If it's dark, step outside or go to a window and find the night sky, even a city one with only a few stars. If it's daytime, look at the sky you have, the light and the clouds, or picture the last starry night you remember. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes go as far as they can. Far beyond what you can see, Lemaître would say, the universe is still growing. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: the heavens declare the glory of God. If you don't, simply look, and let yourself be small for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The priest and the big bang. Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, proposed that the universe is expanding from a beginning, and kept faith and science each in its own lane.
screen: `THE PRIEST AND THE BIG BANG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: faith and science. Today, when you hear the two set against each other, remember a priest at a blackboard who studied the heavens and kept praying. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

Lemaître was a Catholic priest

options: welcome it: the theory proves Genesis.

fork.reveal: Lemaître pushed back. physics describes how the universe unfolds; the Bible, he said, teaches the way to salvation.

trapdoor: what you thought: the church has always been against the big bang.
what it means: the idea of an expanding universe with a beginning was proposed by a Catholic priest.

989.title: Mendel's peas
989.hook: an Augustinian friar in a monastery garden discovers the laws of heredity
989.howItsDone: Some religious orders, the Augustinians among them, keep gardens, schools and libraries alongside their life of prayer, and some of their members have worked as scientists.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a priest at a blackboard and a universe getting bigger. Your line was faith and science. Did you get a look at the sky? Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

Behind the walls of an abbey in Brno, in what is now the Czech Republic, there's a narrow strip of garden. A friar in a dark habit is kneeling in it with a small brush. He is moving pollen from one pea flower to another by hand, then tying a little bag over the flower so no bee can undo his work. He writes everything down. Tall plants, short plants. Smooth peas, wrinkled peas. Yellow, green. Season after season, he plants, crosses, counts and records. His brothers sing the hours in the chapel, and he walks back out to the rows. His name is Gregor Mendel. Today, Mendel's peas.
screen: `A STRIP OF GARDEN BEHIND THE ABBEY.`

segments.voice: Mendel was an Augustinian friar, a member of a religious order that lives by a rule of prayer and shared life. His abbey valued learning, and sent him to study science. What he found in the garden was this: traits from the parent plants don't simply blend together like paint. Cross a tall pea with a short one, and the next generation can all come up tall. The shortness seems gone. But let those tall plants pollinate themselves, and in the next generation short ones come back. Something was being carried, hidden, and passed on, in units that kept their identity from one generation to the next. Today we call those units genes, and the study of them genetics. Mendel didn't have either word. He had peas, patience and a notebook. When he published his results, they drew little notice. He went on to become abbot, busy with the running of the house, and he died before the world caught up with what he'd seen. Later scientists, working on the same questions, found his paper and saw that he had already worked it out in a garden. The Bible's first chapter has an old line about exactly what he was watching. In the King James translation: "the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind." After his kind. Like gives rise to like. Genesis names the pattern; the friar counted how it works, row by row. Paul borrowed a gardener's picture too, writing about the church at Corinth: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." The planter and the waterer do their part, and then they wait. Mendel's whole method was that kind of waiting.

Here's the practice: tend something that grows. If there's a plant near you, go to it. Touch the soil. Is it dry? Water it, or turn it toward the light. If there's no plant, hold a seed, a bean, an apple pip, or simply picture one in your palm. Settle, and breathe. Think about everything packed into that small thing, waiting. You don't make it grow. You only give it what it needs and wait. If you pray, you can say Paul's line: I have planted, but God gave the increase. If you don't, simply stay with the patience of it for the full two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Mendel's peas. The garden experiments of Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, which showed that traits are passed on in units that can hide and return.
Your line: the monk's garden. Today, plant something, or water something already growing, and give it time without checking on it every hour. Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

it drew little notice. later scientists found his paper after his death.
Mendel became abbot of his house

options: decide the shortness is gone for good.
let those tall plants pollinate themselves and see what comes up.
stop the experiment and plant beans.
fork.reveal: Mendel bred from those tall plants, letting them pollinate themselves, and short plants came back. the trait had been hidden, not lost.

original.note: Hebrew: seed — the "herb yielding seed" of Genesis 1:11, also used for descendants.

trapdoor: what you thought: science and monasteries don't mix.
what it means: a friar in an abbey garden worked out how traits pass from parents to offspring.
what a scholar hears: Mendel's units, later called genes, kept their identity across generations; his paper drew little notice until later scientists found it.

sources.ref: Gregor Mendel, Experiments on Plant Hybridization

990.title: Bach's signature
990.hook: Bach signed his scores SDG, to God alone the glory
990.howItsDone: Some Christian musicians, artists and writers still mark their work with S.D.G. or soli Deo gloria, and others dedicate their work to God in a short prayer before they begin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a friar with a brush, moving pollen between pea flowers. Your line was the monk's garden. What did you water, and did you leave it alone to grow? Day nine hundred ninety.

A church musician in Leipzig is up late, finishing a piece for Sunday. Choir parts, organ, strings, a hymn tune running through the middle of it all. He has a congregation to feed and a family to feed, and the deadline is days away, not months. He gets to the last bar, draws the final double line, and then, under the music, he writes three letters. S. D. G. Not his name. Not a date. Three letters, where a signature would go. His name was Johann Sebastian Bach. Today, Bach's signature.

S. D. G. stands for three Latin words: soli Deo gloria. To God alone the glory. It's a short way of saying that the credit for any good thing belongs to God, not to us. Bach was a Lutheran, and he wrote it at the end of scores. At the top of some, he wrote two other letters, J. J., for Jesu juva: Jesus, help. Help at the start, glory at the end. That's the whole shape of a working day in four letters. The idea has a long echo in scripture. The opening of Psalm 115, in the King James Bible: "Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory." Notice the psalmist says not unto us twice. It's hard to mean it the first time. And Paul takes the idea out of the church and into the kitchen: "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." Eat, drink, whatever. Bach didn't save the letters for his grandest works. Tradition says he signed ordinary pieces too, written to a deadline for an ordinary Sunday. And some of his music for keyboard students, teaching pieces, carries a dedication along the same lines. The glory wasn't reserved for the masterpiece. It went on the homework. Bach could be stubborn, and he argued with his employers. The letters weren't a claim to be holy. They were a way of handing the work over when it was done.
screen: `SOLI DEO GLORIA: TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one piece of work to sign. Settle, and breathe. Think through what's ahead of you today. An email. A meal. A shift. A report. A conversation with a child. Pick one ordinary thing. Now picture finishing it, and then, quietly, signing it, the way Bach signed his scores. If you pray, you can write or whisper the letters S. D. G. at the end of it, or say the psalm: not unto us, O Lord. If you don't, you can sign it for the person it serves, and let the credit go. Rest with that for the full two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Bach's signature. The letters S. D. G., soli Deo gloria, to God alone the glory, written by Johann Sebastian Bach at the end of his scores.
Your line: soli deo gloria. Today, finish the one thing you chose, and before you send it or serve it, sign it in your head with three small letters. Day nine hundred ninety.

fork.reveal: Bach wrote S. D. G. under the music: soli Deo gloria. the credit went to God, even on the homework.

991.title: Rembrandt's prodigal
991.hook: an old painter paints the father's two different hands on his son's back
991.howItsDone: Some Christians meditate on paintings of Bible stories as a form of prayer, looking slowly at one image, and Rembrandt's prodigal son is a picture some return to again and again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three letters under the last bar of a score. Your line was soli deo gloria. What did you sign, and who got the credit? Day nine hundred ninety-one.

Most of the canvas is dark. Brown, deep red, shadow. Out of it, light falls on two figures. A young man kneels with his back to us, his head shaved, one shoe off, the other worn through at the heel. His face is pressed into an old man's chest. The old man is bending over him, eyes half closed, and his two hands rest on the young man's back. Off to the right, standing tall in a red cloak, another man watches, and doesn't come closer. Rembrandt painted this late in his life, art historians think, after years of loss. Today, Rembrandt's prodigal.

The story is Jesus's, in the fifteenth chapter of Luke. A younger son takes his share of the inheritance, wastes it, ends up feeding pigs and hungry enough to want their food. He walks home with a speech ready. The King James Bible gives the moment: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." The father runs before the son says a word. Rembrandt doesn't paint the running. He paints what comes after: the son is home, and the father is holding him. Now look at the hands. Viewers have noticed that they aren't a matching pair. One is broad and strong, the fingers spread, pressing. The other is slimmer and smoother, resting more gently. Some readers see a father's hand and a mother's hand. Some see firmness and tenderness together. Rembrandt left no note explaining them, so nobody knows for certain what he meant. But two different hands on one back is hard to miss once you've seen it. And then there's the man in the red cloak. Viewers take him to be the elder brother, the one who stayed home and did everything right, and who in Luke's story stands outside, angry, refusing to come in. The father goes out to him too, and says, "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine." The story ends with the father still speaking. Jesus never says whether the elder brother walked in. Rembrandt leaves him standing in the light, still deciding.
screen: `A GREAT WAY OFF, HIS FATHER RAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the painting. If you can, search for Rembrandt's Return of the Prodigal Son and let it fill your screen. If you can't, use the picture from the start: the dark room, the kneeling son, the old man's two hands. Settle, and breathe. Look first at the hands, one strong, one gentle. Then let your eye drift to the brother in the red cloak. Notice which figure your eye keeps returning to. Don't judge it. Just notice. If you pray, you can rest in the line: his father saw him, and had compassion. If you don't, simply stay with the picture for the full two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Rembrandt's prodigal. The Return of the Prodigal Son, painted by Rembrandt late in life: a father's two different hands on his son's back, and an elder brother watching.
Your line: two hands. Today, when someone comes to you having gotten something wrong, try meeting them with both: one hand that's steady, one that's kind. Day nine hundred ninety-one.

992.title: Handel's Messiah
992.hook: an oratorio sewn together from the King James Bible, first performed for charity in Dublin
992.howItsDone: Choirs and churches perform Messiah each year, especially around Christmas and Easter, and some cities hold sing-along performances where the audience joins the choruses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a dark canvas and a father's two hands on his son's back. Your line was two hands. Who did you meet with one steady hand and one kind one? Day nine hundred ninety-two.

A hall in Dublin, packed. The organizers have asked the ladies not to wear the wide hooped skirts of the day, and the gentlemen to leave their swords at home, so that more people can squeeze in. The money from the tickets is going to charity. On the stage, singers and an orchestra, and a new piece by a German composer living in London, George Frideric Handel. There's no costume, no acting, no plot in the usual sense. Just singers and players and, word after word, the Bible. Today, Handel's Messiah.

Messiah is an oratorio: sacred words set to music for concert singers, without staging. Handel didn't write the words. A friend of his, Charles Jennens, assembled them, by choosing rather than composing. He stitched the text together from the King James Bible and the Prayer Book psalms. Isaiah's comfort ye. The shepherds in the fields. Behold the Lamb of God. I know that my redeemer liveth. It tells the whole story of Christ, from promise to birth to death to rising, using only scripture. At the close of the second section comes the Hallelujah chorus. Its words come from the book of Revelation. In the King James Bible, chapter nineteen: "Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth." And then, from chapter eleven, the line that gives today its carry: "The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever." Handel sets that last phrase so that it comes round again and again, the voices overlapping, as if nobody can quite stop saying it. And there's a custom that goes with it. In some places, audiences stand for the Hallelujah chorus. Tradition says a king once stood at that moment, and everyone stood with him. There's no firm record that it happened. People stand anyway. What they're standing for is a line from the last book of the Bible: the kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord.
screen: `HE SHALL REIGN FOR EVER AND EVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to the Hallelujah chorus. If you can, find a recording and play it. If you can't play anything right now, read the two lines from Revelation slowly to yourself. Settle, and breathe. As it plays, listen for the moment when the words he shall reign for ever and ever start to repeat and overlap. Count how many times you hear it, or don't count, and just let it wash past. If you pray, you can let it be your praise, and stand if you'd like to. If you don't, simply listen to an old, sung claim about whose kingdom lasts. The bell holds the time.
Handel's Messiah. An oratorio by George Frideric Handel, with words drawn entirely from scripture, first performed for charity in Dublin, and remembered for its Hallelujah chorus.
Your line: and he shall reign. Today, when the news feels like the only kingdom there is, hum that one phrase under your breath. Day nine hundred ninety-two.

993.title: Mahalia Jackson
993.hook: the queen of gospel, who sang at the great civil rights march in the capital
993.howItsDone: Gospel music is sung in Black churches across the United States and far beyond, by choirs and soloists in Sunday worship, at funerals and at community gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a packed hall in Dublin and a chorus that won't stop saying it. Your line was and he shall reign. Did you hum it when the news got loud? Day nine hundred ninety-three.

A crowd stretches down the National Mall in the capital, all the way along the reflecting pool. It's hot. There have been speeches all afternoon. Then a woman steps up to the microphones at the Lincoln Memorial, and she doesn't give a speech. She sings. An old spiritual about being scorned and put down, sung slow and huge, and the crowd goes still. A little later, Martin Luther King Jr. is speaking, and the story is told that she called out to him from behind: tell them about the dream, Martin. However it happened, he moved away from his prepared text. Her name was Mahalia Jackson. Today, the woman people called the queen of gospel.

Mahalia Jackson grew up in New Orleans and sang in church from childhood. She moved north to Chicago and kept singing, in storefront churches, at funerals, anywhere they'd have her. Gospel music in that city was being shaped by people like Thomas A. Dorsey, a songwriter who had once played the blues. Dorsey wrote the song that gives today its carry: Precious Lord, Take My Hand. He wrote it, by his own account, out of grief, after his wife and newborn child died. It's a prayer from someone who is tired and can barely stand, asking to be led home. Mahalia Jackson made it one of her signature songs. She was offered good money to sing the blues, and she turned it down. She would sing gospel and nothing else. That song's plea is an old one in scripture. In Isaiah, in the King James Bible, God says: "For I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee." And in Psalm seventy-three, someone who has nearly lost their footing says: "Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand." Hold my hand. A child says it crossing a street. When Martin Luther King Jr. was killed, Mahalia Jackson sang Precious Lord at his funeral. The movement that had marched to her singing now grieved to it. Gospel, the way she sang it, was never only for Sunday. It walked into the street, into the march and into the funeral, and it kept asking for a hand.

Here's the practice: listen to a gospel song. If you can, find Mahalia Jackson singing Precious Lord, Take My Hand, or any gospel recording you like, and let it play. If you can't play anything, read Isaiah's line slowly: I will hold thy right hand, fear not. Settle, and breathe. As you listen, rest one hand open on your knee. Notice where in your life you'd like a hand to hold right now. If you pray, you can let the song carry your own asking. If you don't, simply listen to a woman singing for people who were tired, and let it be two minutes of company. The bell holds the time.

Mahalia Jackson. A gospel singer from New Orleans and Chicago, called the queen of gospel, who sang at the Lincoln Memorial during the great march for jobs and freedom and sang Precious Lord at Martin Luther King Jr.'s funeral.
Your line: precious lord. Today, find someone who's running on empty and carry a little of the load: a ride, a call, a meal dropped off. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

994.title: Flannery O'Connor
994.hook: a Southern writer whose strange stories find grace in grotesque places
994.howItsDone: O'Connor's stories are read in classrooms, book groups and church study circles, where Christians talk about how grace can come through hard or strange moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman singing at the Lincoln Memorial, and a song asking for a hand. Your line was precious lord. Whose load did you carry a little of? Day nine hundred ninety-four.

A doctor's waiting room in the South. A respectable woman named Mrs. Turpin sits sizing everyone up: who's trashy, who's decent, who's beneath her. She's thanking Jesus, privately, that she was made the way she was. Across the room, a sullen college girl is glaring at her over a book. And then, without warning, the girl throws the book. It hits Mrs. Turpin in the face. The girl lunges at her, calls her an old wart hog and tells her to go back to hell. It's a scene from a short story called Revelation, and it's funny and awful at once. The writer was Flannery O'Connor. Today, a Catholic storyteller from Georgia.

Flannery O'Connor spent her later years on a family farm in Georgia, raising peacocks and living with lupus, the illness that had taken her father. She was a devout Catholic, and she wrote stories full of con men, killers, prophets, and very proper people who are much less proper than they think. Her characters are often ugly, violent or ridiculous. Readers have sometimes asked why a writer of faith would write such grim, odd stories. Her answer, put plainly in her letters and essays, was that grace often arrives as a shock, and that her characters were too sure of themselves to notice it any other way. So the book in Mrs. Turpin's face is not the end of the story. That evening, hosing down her pigs, she argues with God out loud. And then she sees something. A procession stretching up into the sky, a vast crowd on its way to heaven. At the front, the people she looked down on, singing and leaping. At the back, people like her, decent and orderly, still singing on key, but with shocked faces, their virtues being burned away. Jesus told the respectable leaders of his day something like this. In Matthew, in the King James Bible: "the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you." And Paul writes: "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise." O'Connor's stories rarely end with anyone tidy. They end with someone struck, and seeing, maybe for the first time. Grace, in her fiction, doesn't knock politely. It throws the book.
screen: `A CATHOLIC WRITER ON A GEORGIA FARM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for grace in someone odd. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who gets under your skin. Not someone dangerous, just someone strange, loud, awkward, hard to like. A neighbor, a coworker, a relative at the holidays. Picture their face. Now look for one thing in them you missed. Something they carry. Something they do well. Something they might be hoping for. If you pray, you can hold them before God, just as they are. If you don't, simply let them be more than your first impression for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Flannery O'Connor. A Catholic writer from Georgia whose strange, often violent stories show grace breaking into the lives of people who are sure they don't need it.
Your line: grace in odd places. This week ran from a priest at a blackboard to a farm full of peacocks. Today, when someone strikes you as strange, look twice. Day nine hundred ninety-four.

myth: O'Connor's stories are gentle and sweet
they're full of con men, killers and proper people who aren't. grace arrives as a shock.
in Revelation, Mrs. Turpin sees the people she looked down on going first
at the front of the procession, singing and leaping; people like her come last.
Jesus told respectable leaders that publicans and harlots would enter the kingdom before them
"the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you."

fork.setup: you're Mrs. Turpin. a stranger has just thrown a book at you and called you an old wart hog and told you to go back to hell. that evening, alone with your pigs, what do you do?
options: forget it; she was clearly disturbed.
argue with God out loud about it.
call the girl's mother to complain.
fork.reveal: she argues with God, hosing down the pigs, and then sees a procession to heaven with the people she looked down on going first.

original.note: Greek: grace, an unearned gift — the word Paul uses for God's favor.

trapdoor: what you thought: dark Southern stories with no faith in them.
what it means: stories by a Catholic writer where grace breaks in through violence and embarrassment.
what a scholar hears: O'Connor's own explanation that her characters needed a shock to see; Revelation ends with the looked-down-on going first, as in Matthew 21:31.

sources.ref: Flannery O'Connor, Mystery and Manners; The Habit of Being
